summary:
Gauteng stands under the national constitutional framework of the Republic of South Africa. The Constitution of 1996 prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. Sexual-orientation discrimination was banned in 1996, making South Africa the first country to do so; marriage equality followed with the Civil Union Act of 2006; legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003; and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics.

On 10 November 2025 the Gauteng Division of the High Court, sitting as an Equality Court, delivered judgment in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (case 2024/070075), a challenge against the Department of Correctional Services brought with the assistance of Lawyers for Human Rights. The court found that the Department engaged in unfair discrimination and harassment of a transgender inmate by refusing to let her express her gender identity and by denying prescribed gender-affirming hormone therapy. It held that the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at state expense. Orders compelling the Department to provide hormone treatment, permit clothing and cosmetics expressing the inmate's gender identity, implement its own standard operating procedure for transgender inmates, and deliver prescribed medical care were granted. The South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism welcomed the ruling on 14 November 2025.

The judgment is the only documented determination of where trans prisoners are housed in Gauteng. Mokoena, a transgender woman serving a life sentence at Johannesburg Correctional Centre, was initially held in the Medium A section, where she could express her gender identity through long hair, make-up and women's clothing, and was later transferred to Medium C. At the time of judgment she was held in C Single Section, a segregated unit of Medium C, accommodated with cisgender male cellmates despite requesting a single cell; the Department justified this by overcrowding. The court found no basis for refusing single accommodation and ordered the Department to house her in a single cell or with inmates of the same gender identity, and to enforce its transgender-inmate standard operating procedure.

Correctional Services already had a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners before the ruling; reporting in August 2025 recorded that rights organisations doubt whether it is implemented in practice. Detention therefore remains a site of elevated risk for trans visitors and residents in Gauteng despite the binding remedies now in place.

Outside prison, everyday exposure is shaped by documents. The Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act requires medical evidence, a pathologising route that locks people out of legal gender recognition, and its binary sex classification excludes non-binary people altogether; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force. The costs of affirming one's gender through the process are described as dauntingly high. Where documents do not match presentation, trans people face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 Gender Dynamix report documents a trans woman who was met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

Violence risk is documented and ongoing. On 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old trans woman and make-up artist from Soshanguve living in Winterveld, both in Tshwane, was assaulted at a tavern at about 1:30 am after a man said gay and lesbian people do not deserve to live. He smashed a bottle into her face as she lit a cigarette, saying he was going to kill her, leaving deep cuts to her mouth, lips, nose, cheek and forehead that were stitched at Kgabo Clinic. She opened an assault case at Dube Police Station, which was reported on 6 January 2025 to have shown no progress. This is the province's most recent documented trans-specific hate incident on record. OUT LGBT Well-being's rights watch for December 2024 recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders that month, and violence disproportionately affects Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in townships.

Gauteng was the subject of the first representative quantitative provincial hate-crime study in South Africa, conducted in 2003/04 by OUT LGBT Well-being with the University of South Africa's Centre for Applied Psychology (Wells and Polders) under the Joint Working Group research initiative, with partners including Behind the Mask, Triangle Project, GALA and the Durban Lesbian & Gay Community & Health Centre.

Academic analysis published in 2024 examining whether PEPUDA read with section 9 of the Constitution prohibits the exclusion of transgender and non-binary people from gender-segregated bathrooms concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable for visitors.
tangentialFactors:
The national evidence base on hate crimes against LGBT people is thin. The 2016 Love Not Hate campaign research, conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being and hosted by GALA, records that only three quantitative studies on the subject have ever been done in South Africa: a 2003 empowerment study covering Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and Western Cape, a 2010 North West province study, and the national campaign study itself. Provincial prevalence figures for Gauteng therefore rest largely on a two-decade-old baseline.

Access to gender-affirming care is uneven nationally. Activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over treatment delays running to a year, an Eastern Cape example that indicates waiting times a Gauteng visitor may also encounter rather than a Gauteng facility finding.
localsOnly:
Residents can invoke PEPUDA through the Equality Court, and the Mokoena judgment demonstrates an operational Gauteng remedy under that statute for discrimination against a trans person, including an order that the Department of Correctional Services fund gender-affirming hormonal therapy and enforce its own standard operating procedure for transgender inmates.

Legal gender recognition under the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act remains available but requires medical evidence, and the process is described as prohibitively expensive for many applicants. Reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force, and the binary classification offers no route for non-binary residents.

Provincial advocacy and research infrastructure includes OUT LGBT Well-being, which conducted both the 2003/04 provincial hate-crime study with the University of South Africa's Centre for Applied Psychology and the 2016 national Love Not Hate research, alongside partner organisations Behind the Mask, Triangle Project, GALA and the Durban Lesbian & Gay Community & Health Centre.
outOfScopeNotes:
The date of the Mokoena judgment is reported inconsistently across sources: the South African Human Rights Commission's statement gives 10 November 2025 as the delivery date and 14 November 2025 as the date its National Preventive Mechanism welcomed it, while other framing places delivery on 14 November. The discrepancy is unresolved here.

Whether the Department of Correctional Services' standard operating procedure for transgender inmates is implemented in practice is unresolved; rights organisations voiced doubt in August 2025 reporting, and the November 2025 order to enforce it postdates that reporting.

The progress of the criminal case opened at Dube Police Station over the December 2024 assault on Aobakwe Mahlobo was reported as showing no movement as of 6 January 2025; no later outcome is sourced.

Current provincial counts of anti-trans violence beyond the December 2024 national tally of five LGBTQIA+ murders are not sourced, and no Gauteng-specific figure for that period appears in the inventory.
